t.4.21.1: Then Hanūmān, leader of the monkey troops, gently consoled Tārā, who had fallen to the ground like a star dropped from the sky.
t.4.21.3: You who are yourself to be pitied, whom do you pity as pitiable? Wretched yourself, you feel compassion for one who is wretched. Who indeed is to be mourned by whom, in this body that is like a bubble?
t.4.21.2: After death, a living being calmly obtains all of it, good and bad, which is produced by his virtues and faults and has the fruit of his own deeds as its cause.
t.4.21.4: But this prince Aṅgada must be looked after by you, a mother whose son still lives; and consider what fitting things should be done for his future.
t.4.21.5: You know thus that the coming and going of beings is uncertain. Therefore, for one who is wise, what is auspicious is indeed to be done, not what pertains merely to this world.
t.4.21.6: He on whom thousands, millions and hundreds of millions of monkeys depended for their livelihood, each having been assigned his share, has now met his destined end.
t.4.21.7: Since he, who understood matters through right reasoning and was devoted to conciliation, generosity and forbearance, has gone to the realm won by righteousness, you ought not to grieve for him.
t.4.21.8: All these tiger-like monkeys, this son of yours, Aṅgada, and the kingdom of the lord of monkeys and bears now have you as their protector, O blameless lady.
t.4.21.9: Gently guide these two, who are scorched with grief, O lovely lady. Under your care, let this Aṅgada rule the earth.
t.4.21.10: Let the succession be settled as has been ordained, and whatever is now to be done for the king, let all of that be done; this is the decree of time.
t.4.21.11: The king of the monkeys must now receive his funeral rites, and let Aṅgada be consecrated as king; beholding your son seated upon the throne, you will find peace.
t.4.21.12: Having heard his words, Tārā, afflicted by the calamity that had befallen her husband, gave a reply to Hanumān, who stood before her.
t.4.21.13: On one side stand a hundred sons like Aṅgada; on the other, the embrace of this hero's body, though he lies slain, and that embrace is better.
t.4.21.14: I have no authority over the king of the monkeys, nor over Aṅgada; for the one whose father has been struck down, Sugrīva is the nearest in all matters.
t.4.21.15: O Hanumān, such a thought must not be entertained concerning Aṅgada, for it is the father who is the true kinsman of a son, not the mother, O best of monkeys.
t.4.21.16: For me there is nothing more fitting, in the world beyond or here, than shelter with the king of the monkeys; this bed, resorted to by heroes slain while facing the foe, is fitting for me to share.
